meta.description: Eskom residential tariff components, used by the shadow dynamic retail price panel. Every figure is from Eskom's published Schedule of Standard Prices; nothing here is modelled.
meta.source: Eskom Schedule of Standard Prices for the 2026/27 financial year, effective 1 April 2026, published after NERSA's MYPD6 decision of 5 March 2026. Direct-customer rates, 8.76% average increase.
meta.vat: All figures INCLUDE VAT at 15% unless a field name says otherwise.
meta.phase_in: Eskom is moving residential cost recovery from energy charges to fixed charges over three years. Service and administration went from 33.33% fixed in FY2026 to 66.66% in FY2027. The Generation Capacity Charge went from 20% to 30%. The remainder of each sits inside the energy charge. The ERTSA application for 2027/28, gazetted 4 Sep 2026, continues this.
meta.why_this_file_exists: The shadow retail price needs the components a household actually pays, not a single average rate. It also lets the fixed/variable split be modelled as a scenario rather than asserted - see the frozen and completed cases in RESULTS.md.
meta.caveat_municipal: Homepower and Homelight are ESKOM DIRECT tariffs. Municipal customers buy from their distributor at a bulk rate and pay that distributor's own structure and markup, which varies by an order of magnitude between metros. Do not present an Eskom-direct figure as a national household price.

homepower4.description: Standard residential, 80 A single-phase, no grid-tied generation. The most common Eskom-direct residential tariff.
homepower4.energy_note: Flat rate. The same at 03:00 as at 18:00, and the same in July as in January. This is the quantity a dynamic tariff would replace.

phase_in_status.note: At 100% the service and administration charge is R9.90/day and the generation capacity charge R2.73/day. R5.21/day, about R159/month, has still to move from energy to fixed.

homepower4.fixed_r_per_month_note: R17.86/day x 30 = R535.8, quoted as R536. Eskom bills per day, so a 31-day month is R553.7 and a 28-day month R500.1. The monthly figure is a convenience for comparison, not a charge - use fixed_r_per_day for anything computed.
homepower4.energy_is_not_pure_energy: R3.5556/kWh still carries 33.34% of the service and administration charge and 70% of the generation capacity charge, both mid phase-in. So any tariff anchored to this rate inherits some fixed-cost recovery inside its energy component. That is not an error - it is what a household actually pays per unit today - but it means the anchor is not a pure energy price.

homeflex.description: Time-of-use residential. Required for any household with grid-tied generation, so every rooftop PV customer is on it. Same network, retail and ancillary charges as Homepower; only the energy charges differ.
homeflex.source: NERSA Reasons for Decision, Eskom Electricity Retail Tariff Plan, 18 Feb 2025, Table 7. Proposed rates in 2024/25 rand, adjusted to 2026/27 by the approved ERTSA increases.
homeflex.ratio_note: NERSA approved a change from 1:8 to 1:6 in Feb 2025. The 4.4x spread previously quoted here came from two rates only and was a winter figure; the full six-rate table is now present and the annual spread can be computed properly.
homeflex.all_six_rates_note: PREVIOUSLY ONLY THE WINTER PAIR WAS HELD, and the panel had to caveat that its Homeflex comparison was a high-demand-season figure. Resolved 10 Sep 2026 from the NERSA decision document.

homelight60a.description: Residential prepaid, 60A. No fixed charge. Also cross-subsidised, less than the 20A.
homelight60a.source: NERSA Reasons for Decision, 18 Feb 2025, Table 11.
homelight60a.note: Beats Homepower at every realistic consumption for eligible households because it has no fixed charge to absorb - and because it is subsidised.

reference_octopus_agile.description: Britain's most-cited dynamic tariff, included as a published comparator rather than a target. Its formula is public, which is the standard this model holds itself to.
reference_octopus_agile.structure: day-ahead wholesale, half-hourly, plus regional network costs, plus a peak uplift, plus margin, plus VAT, subject to a cap
reference_octopus_agile.note: The standing charge is NOT dynamic. That is the honest limit on what any dynamic tariff can shift, and it matters more in South Africa: a 200 kWh Homepower household is already at 43% fixed against Octopus's 24%.

shadow_tariff_parameters.description: The four parameters the shadow dynamic tariff needs that Eskom does not publish. Each is sourced; two are South African observations and two are imported from markets that actually run dynamic tariffs.
shadow_tariff_parameters.municipal_markup_basis: Midpoint of the observed Cape Town range. A Cape Town household typically pays R3.80-5.20/kWh on the standard block against R3.22/kWh for an Eskom-direct Homepower customer, so 18-61%; the midpoint is 40%. For scale: PowerForum found Ekurhuleni at 86%, the highest in the country, and Steyn (2004) put cost-reflective distributor profit at 10-20% on roughly 10% technical losses. 40% therefore sits between what cost recovery justifies and what the worst case charges. EXPOSE THIS AS A SLIDER - the spread between metros is an order of magnitude and no single figure describes the country.
shadow_tariff_parameters.cap_basis: Octopus Agile caps at 100 p/kWh against an Ofgem standard-variable cap of 27.69 p/kWh for Jan-Mar 2026, a ratio of 3.6x. Applying the same ratio to Homepower 4's flat energy rate of R3.5556/kWh gives R12.84. Octopus states the reason plainly: their wholesale can exceed 200 p/kWh at peak and without a cap 'the peak rates would get totally extortionate for a domestic customer'. Our shortage hours price at the value of lost load, around R80,000/MWh, so an uncapped pass-through would be absurd rather than merely high.
shadow_tariff_parameters.retail_margin_basis: IMPORTED. South Africa has no competitive retail supply, so there is no domestic margin to observe. European dynamic tariffs - Tibber, aWATTar, Octopus - add 1 to 3 euro-cents per kWh plus a monthly fee. At roughly R20 to the euro that is R0.20 to R0.60; R0.30 is the low-middle. This is the single most assumption-laden number in the panel and should be labelled as such wherever it appears.
shadow_tariff_parameters.peak_uplift_note: Octopus adds 10-14 p/kWh between 16:00 and 19:00 on top of wholesale, because the network cost of the evening peak is real and separate from the energy cost. We do NOT add one: our transmission cost is already carried in txRPerKWyr and the Eskom network capacity charge is in the fixed component, so adding an uplift would double-count. Stated here because its absence is a deliberate choice, not an oversight.
shadow_tariff_parameters.wind_shape_caveat: The modelled wind profile's daily shape is imperfect - its trough sits four hours early against Eskom's metered fleet. Measured effect on this panel: applying the full three-hour correction moves the daily price shape by a 0.967 correlation and R18/MWh on a R808 mean, about 2%. Wind is only 12.9% of the daily net-load swing; demand and solar set the shape. Small, but state it.

allowed_revenue_2026_27.description: NERSA's approved allowed revenue and Eskom's own decomposition of it. This is the skeleton of a retail tariff: a revenue requirement, split into components, recovered per kWh. The panel builds the shadow price bottom-up from these rather than anchoring to a published tariff.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.source: NERSA MYPD6 decision of 30 Jan 2025 and the 2026 settlement: approved total revenue R384,610m for 2025/26. The component split is Eskom's own published revenue build-up for the same year, which totals R444.7bn as APPLIED FOR; NERSA approved 86.5% of it, and each component below is scaled by that factor.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.caveat: CORRECTED 10 Sep 2026. The first version applied the build-up shares to NERSA's GENERATION allowance alone. That was wrong - Eskom's build-up is the whole company and already contains transmission and distribution. Applying whole-company shares to one business inflated every component by 1.72x. Check any component against the R2.016/kWh total before trusting it.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.sales_basis: CORRECTED 10 Sep 2026. Was 190.81, which is DISPATCHABLE energy sent out and excludes wind and solar IPPs. Eskom recovers its revenue over what it sells: RSA contracted energy demand, 2025, from the Weekly System Status Report annual table. The change lowers every per-kWh component by 9%.

how_each_responds_to_a_scenario.primary_energy_fuel: MODELLED. Taken from the dispatch run's fuelCost, not from this table.
how_each_responds_to_a_scenario.ipp_purchases: Scales with renewable capacity - more build means more PPAs to honour.
how_each_responds_to_a_scenario.operating_costs: Scales with retained coal capacity. Fewer stations, less to operate.
how_each_responds_to_a_scenario.depreciation: Existing fleet: see stranded_asset_treatment. New build: from the run's newCapexR.
how_each_responds_to_a_scenario.rca_recoveries: Fixed. A historical clawback, unaffected by what is built.
how_each_responds_to_a_scenario.arrear_debt: Fixed. Municipal arrears, unaffected by what is built.

stranded_asset_treatment.description: THE DECISION THAT DRIVES THE ANSWER. When coal retires early, what happens to the depreciation and return on assets still attached to it?
stranded_asset_treatment.stranded: Consumers keep paying until the asset base runs off. This is what a regulated asset base actually does, and NERSA's R54bn RAB correction in 2025-26 shows how live the question is. Retail prices RISE under aggressive decarbonisation.
stranded_asset_treatment.written_off: The cost leaves with the plant. Someone still pays, usually the fiscus. Retail prices FALL.
stranded_asset_treatment.why_it_is_a_control: Same physics, different regulatory assumption, opposite conclusions. Picking one quietly would make the panel an argument rather than a tool.

allowed_revenue_2026_27.business_r_million_note: Kept for reference only. Generation R258,574m and NTCSA R109,289m are NERSA's approved 2026/27 figures; distribution is the residual of Eskom's application and is NOT approved. The panel uses the component split above, not this three-way split, because the components are what respond to a scenario.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.coal_share_basis: Generation is R258,574m of NERSA's R384,610m allowed revenue, 67%. Coal is roughly 80% of generation assets by value once Koeberg, pumped storage and the peakers are taken out. So about 54% of depreciation and return on assets is coal-specific. The written-off case scales ONLY this share with the coal fraction; the first version scaled all of it and wrote off the transmission network when coal retired.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.new_build_fixed_om_basis: Fixed O&M, NOT in acap* which is annualised capex only. Mid-range of NREL ATB and South African REIPPPP disclosures: wind R600-900, utility PV R250-400, batteries R300-500, CCGT R250-350 per kW-year. Missing from the first build entirely; on the Future electricity mix it is worth about R0.24/kWh.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.decommissioning_basis: Closure and rehabilitation of retired coal plant, annualised. Komati was budgeted at roughly R8bn for a 1 GW station including repurposing, but most of that is the repurposing. Bare closure and rehabilitation is nearer R1,000-2,000/kW. Someone pays it in both the stranded and written-off cases; it is added to both. ASSUMPTION - no South African fleet-wide figure is published.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.opex_coal_share_basis: ASSUMPTION. Of Eskom's operating costs, R37bn is employee benefits and the rest is largely maintenance, both concentrated in generation. 60% is taken as coal-station-specific and falls with retirement; 40% is the network and corporate base that does not. Plausible, unsourced, and moves the result by less than the items above.

scenario_year.description: Parameters that key off the panel's scenario year. Reference practice: AEMO's ISP reports target-year snapshots; Ofgem rolls the regulated asset base forward annually; NERSA's MYPD does it in three-year windows. GridTwin's dispatch stays a single representative year at the chosen date.
scenario_year.rca_basis: The regulatory clearing account claws back past variances over a fixed window. The current tranche - including the R54bn RAB correction recovered over three years - ends with MYPD6 in 2027/28. NERSA settlement, April 2026.
scenario_year.arrears_basis: Municipal arrear debt is a transfer from paying customers to non-paying ones, not a cost of supplying electricity. Reference cost-reflective tariff models exclude it. Exposed as a toggle rather than deleted; default excluded.
scenario_year.runoff_basis: The existing fleet's depreciation and return run off as plant ages. Most coal is past half its regulatory life; Medupi and Kusile are not, and neither are the wires. A linear run-off from 100% in 2026 to a 35% floor by 2045 approximates the long-lived residual. ASSUMPTION - NERSA publishes the RAB by business in each MYPD decision and the schedule should be read from there.
scenario_year.vintage_basis: A fleet costed at 2035 was not all bought in 2035. Reference practice prices each vintage at its commissioning year and sums. Without a build pathway the honest approximation is the midpoint between the base year and the scenario year. Stated on the panel.

allowed_revenue_2026_27.eskom_retail_distribution_basis: The last-mile share of Eskom Distribution: the reticulation, metering and customer service a municipal distributor provides for itself. NERSA's approved distribution allowance is about R0.61/kWh over 209.55 TWh; roughly half is sub-transmission and bulk supply that a municipality still buys from Eskom, and roughly half is the retail function it replaces. Removed from the cost base for a municipal customer, who pays their own municipality for it through the markup. ASSUMPTION on the 50/50 split - NERSA publishes distribution allowances but not this cut.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.tdp_grid_basis: Eskom's Transmission Development Plan is R390bn for 56 GW of connection capacity, R6,964m per GW. The model's own connection rate gives about a third of that, and its cost decomposition already labels transmission 'partial'. The panel now annualises the TDP rate over 40 years at 8% against the scenario's new wind and PV, which is the published figure rather than an inferred one.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.residential_allocation_basis: NERSA's allowed revenue is an average across ALL customers. Residential pays well above it: Eskom's average standard-tariff price for 2026/27 is 240.28 c/kWh while Homepower 4's energy charge is 309.2 c/kWh excluding VAT - a 29% premium. That is cost-to-serve, and every regulator allocates it: low voltage, low load factor, and metering and billing spread over few units. Large industrial customers on Megaflex pay BELOW the average for the same reason in reverse. FOUND 10 Sep 2026 when the municipal markup became a switch: with the markup removed for an Eskom-direct customer the panel came out 25% under Homepower, which showed the 40% markup had been silently carrying this allocation as well as a municipal margin.

cts_allocation.description: Eskom's Cost to Serve study allocates NERSA's allowable revenue to customer categories on cost-causation principles: supply voltage, location density, load profile, and number of points of delivery.
cts_allocation.source: NERSA Reasons for Decision, Eskom Retail Tariff Plan, 18 Feb 2025, sections 8.1 and 8.9.
cts_allocation.legacy_charge_note: The premium paid to section 34 REIPPPP contracts above Eskom's own generation cost. Ring-fenced as a separate c/kWh charge from 2025/26, and not applied to Homelight.
cts_allocation.nersa_concern: NERSA found the CTS functionalises allowable revenue as 86/4/10 across Generation, NTCSA and Distribution, against its own MYPD6 apportionment of 62/28/10. It called this a material inconsistency and imposed ring-fencing conditions. So the CTS allocation is published but NOT endorsed by the regulator as consistent with MYPD6 - use it for the customer-category split, not for the business split.

allowed_revenue_2026_27.rca_schedule_basis: The R54bn RAB settlement is liquidated on a PUBLISHED schedule, not a single expiry: R12bn in 2026/27, R23bn in 2027/28 and R19.7bn thereafter. Parliament's Committee on Electricity and Energy briefing, NERSA, 2026. Tariff impact 3.4% in 2026/27 and 2.64% in 2027/28 - the difference between the original 5.36% and the final 8.76%. Replaces the single rca_ends_fy cutoff, which treated a three-year taper as a cliff.
allowed_revenue_2026_27.rab_note: The generation RAB itself is still not published at a level that supports a real depreciation schedule. NERSA's redetermination approved the depreciated replacement cost approach and revalued the generation RAB, but the Reasons for Decision give the revenue effect rather than the asset base and its remaining life. So the run-off below stays a linear approximation. What WOULD close it: the MYPD6 revenue decision tables, which are a separate document from the Retail Tariff Plan.

cross_subsidies.description: Eskom's tariffs contain explicit cross-subsidies. These are TRANSFERS between customer categories, not costs of supply, and a cost-reflective shadow tariff should show them separately rather than fold them into a cost.
cross_subsidies.source: NERSA Reasons for Decision, Eskom Retail Tariff Plan, 18 Feb 2025, Table 15 and section 8.14.
cross_subsidies.payers: Urban large power users pay the electrification and rural subsidy; non-local-authority urban LPUs pay the affordability subsidy.
cross_subsidies.homepower_note: HOMEPOWER IS NOT ON THE SUBSIDISED LIST. It contributes to the affordability subsidy rather than receiving it. So part of the residential premium over Eskom's average price is Homepower funding Homelight - a transfer, not a cost to serve. This corrects an assumption made on 10 Sep 2026 that attributed the whole premium to cost causation.
cross_subsidies.nersa_reduction: NERSA approved reducing the electrification and rural subsidy by 69% and the affordability subsidy by 53%, to relieve large power users.

homelight20a.description: Residential lifeline tariff, 20A prepaid. No fixed charge. The largest recipient of cross-subsidy.
homelight20a.source: NERSA Reasons for Decision, 18 Feb 2025, Table 11. Flat rate replacing the inclining block structure.
homelight20a.note: The legacy charge is NOT applied to Homelight, so REIPPPP premium costs are borne by other categories.
